intro: Skateboarding is a sport, but it is also a culture with its own art, photography, film, music and ways of welcoming people. Deck graphics by artists such as Jim Phillips and Vernon Courtland Johnson hang in shops and homes. Magazines such as SkateBoarder, Thrasher and TransWorld, and videos from The Bones Brigade Video Show to today's online clips, taught people how to skate and what skating could mean.

This unit also asks who got to be part of that culture and who was left out of the pictures. Women such as Patti McGee and Peggy Oki skated from the early years. Skaters of color such as Ray Barbee, Stevie Williams and Nyjah Huston, skaters in Brazil and Japan, and wheelchair riders such as Aaron Fotheringham pushed the doors wider. Groups like Skateistan and The Skatepark Project work on purpose to bring new people in.

By the end you will be able to name key artists, magazines and videos and place them in time, explain how photos and video changed the way people learn tricks, and describe the people and groups who made skateboarding more open. You will also be able to name practical habits that help a skatepark welcome everyone, whether you are watching, starting out or coming back.
bigQuestion: How did skaters build an art world of their own, and how did that world open its doors to more kinds of people?

timeline.t: The Quarterly Skateboarder, the first skate magazine, appears
Patti McGee wins the women's national title and is on the cover of Life
Peggy Oki and the Zephyr team skate the Del Mar Nationals
Thrasher magazine starts in San Francisco
Powell Peralta releases The Bones Brigade Video Show
Skaters begin building Burnside under a Portland bridge
Blind releases Video Days, directed by Spike Jonze
Elissa Steamer is the first woman in Tony Hawk's Pro Skater
Tokyo 2020 Games: teenage women win street and park medals
Paris 2024: Horigome repeats in street; Leal and Huston win bronze

words.d: the art printed on a skateboard deck, usually on the bottom
a deck sold under a professional skater's name, with that skater's own graphic
the Powell Peralta skate team of the 1980s, including Tony Hawk, Steve Caballero and Rodney Mullen
a row of photos taken a fraction of a second apart that shows a trick from start to finish
one skater's own section of a skate video, usually set to a song
a small homemade magazine, often photocopied and stapled, made without a publisher
short for do it yourself; making zines, ramps or parks without waiting for a company or city
who is shown in photos, videos and media, and how they are shown
a series of tricks done one after another in a single run, without stopping
short for wheelchair motocross; riding skatepark ramps and bowls in a wheelchair
changing equipment or the way a skill is done so it fits a person's body
the unwritten rules for sharing a skatepark, such as taking turns and looking before you roll

test.q: Which artist drew skulls and the skull-and-sword design for Powell Peralta?
test.why: Vernon Courtland Johnson (VCJ) drew Powell Peralta's skulls and team graphics.

test.q: Why is most deck art printed on the bottom of the board?
choices: The bottom is made of plastic
Contest judges look only at the bottom
Art on top makes the board slower
test.why: Grip tape covers the top so shoes do not slip, leaving the bottom for art.

test.q: Which magazine began in San Francisco in 1981?
test.why: Thrasher started in San Francisco in 1981.

test.q: Who directed The Bones Brigade Video Show (1984)?
test.why: Stacy Peralta directed Powell Peralta's videos.

test.q: What is the ender of a video part?
choices: The last and usually hardest trick
test.why: The ender closes a part and is usually the hardest or most surprising trick.

test.q: What did online video (YouTube in 2005, Instagram in 2010) change?
choices: Skaters could share clips worldwide without being chosen first
It made VHS the main format
test.why: Posting online let anyone share clips quickly with the world.

test.q: Which music shaped many skaters' culture in the early 1980s?
test.why: Punk's fast, make-it-yourself attitude fit skating in the early 1980s.

test.q: Burnside skatepark in Portland is a famous example of what?
choices: A park built by a design firm in 1965
A DIY park built by skaters, later accepted by the city
test.why: Skaters began building Burnside without permission in 1990, and the city later accepted it.

test.q: Who won the women's title at the first national championships in 1965?
test.why: Patti McGee won the women's national title in Anaheim in 1965.

test.q: Who was the first woman in the game Tony Hawk's Pro Skater?
test.why: Elissa Steamer was the first woman in the 1999 game.

test.q: Who won women's street silver for Brazil at Tokyo 2020 at age 13?
test.why: Rayssa Leal won women's street silver at Tokyo at 13.

test.q: Which skater started his own company, DGK, after becoming known at Love Park?
test.why: Stevie Williams of Philadelphia started DGK in the early 2000s.

test.q: What did Aaron Fotheringham land in the mid-2000s?
test.why: Fotheringham, a WCMX rider, landed the first wheelchair backflip.

test.q: Which of these lowers a barrier for a new skater?
test.why: Loaner gear removes cost as a barrier to starting.

test.q: Which habit is part of good park etiquette?
choices: Taking turns and looking before you roll
test.why: Taking turns and checking your path keeps a park safe for everyone.

write.prompt: Choose one artist, photographer, video or skater from this unit. Explain what they made or did, when, and how it changed skateboarding's art or opened the door for more people. Use at least two dates and two names from the unit.
tips: Start with one clear sentence naming your person or work and its year.
Describe what it looked like or what happened, using a key word such as pro model, sequence or WCMX.
Explain who was affected and how skating changed afterward.
End with what a skater or park today can learn from it.
